body.p: Applicant has reviewed the final Office action dated April 26, 2023, and the references cited therein. Claims 1-13 and 16 are currently pending. Claim 16 is withdrawn from consideration. Claims 1-13 stand rejected. Claims 14-15 are canceled. Applicant's Amendments

Applicant, in view of the current rejection over the teachings of Mahajan, has amended independent claim 1 to further clarify the nature of the claimed first and second signals provided by respective, distinct, electrodes. The two physically distinct (first and second) conductive electrodes operate substantially in a same way (i.e. receiving electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling monitoring of a membrane potential of one or more muscles in the body).
In particular, Applicant's claim 1 now recites:
A wearable device for monitoring one or more vital signs of a human
body, the wearable device comprising:
a carrier configured to fit, while in use, fully around the human body, at an
abdominal part thereof; and
an electrode arrangement comprising a plurality of conductive electrodes

including one or more first electrode and one or more second electrode, wherein the plurality of conductive electrodes are arranged on the carrier to be brought in contact with a skin of the body in use, and wherein all electrodes of the plurality of conductive electrodes are configured for operating simultaneously to receive
electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling monitoring of a
membrane potential of one or more muscles in the body,
wherein the one or more first electrode is arranged on the carrier to be in
contact with a side part of a torso of the body near the thoracic diaphragm, the one
or more first electrode being configured to cooperatively receive a first electrical
signal indicative of a membrane potential of a thoracic diaphragm of the body and
for providing the first electrical signal as a measurement signal;
wherein each electrode of the one or more second electrode and the one
or more first electrode is arranged aligned on the belt, such that the one or more second electrode is aligned with the one or more first electrode, the at least one
second electrode thereby being arranged for receiving a second electrical signal
indicative of one or more further electric physiologic signals from the body,
wherein the second electrical signal in particular is indicative of a
further membrane potential, and
wherein the one or more second electrode is arranged for providing the
second electrical signal separate from the first electrical signal, the second
electrode thereby providing a filter signal, for enabling filtering of the first
electrical signal using the second electrical signal for enabling electromyography
of the thoracic diaphragm. (Emphasis added).

Support for the current clarifying claim text is provided in Applicant's original application's description of electrodes 19 and 20 that are identified as EMG electrodes that operate in substantially the same manner to facilitate obtaining an ECG signal. See Applicant's specification, page 12, lines 7-9; page 12, line 22 to page 13, line 12; page 13, lines 13-15; and page 14, lines 1-2.
Applicant requests favorable reconsideration of the grounds for rejection of the

previously pending claims in view of Applicant's further amendments to the claims and remarks addressing the shortcomings of the prior art with regard to particular recited elements of the claimed invention.
Please charge any fee deficiencies to Deposit Account No. 12-1216. Grounds for Rejecting the Claims
1. Claims 1-5 and 11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Mahajan, WO 2015/175904 (Mahajan).
2. Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and in view of McGrane, U.S. Pub. No. 2017/0019988 (McGrane).
3. Claim 7 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and in view of Maesani, U.S. Pub. No. 2017/0273590 (Maesani).
4. Claims 8 and 10 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over
Mahajan in view of Maesani as applied to claim 7 and in further view of Muccio, U.S. Pub. No. 2012/0016440 (Muccio).
5. Claim 9 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and in view of Hsiao, U.S. Pub. No. 2012/0265025 (Hsiao).
6. Claim 12 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Sims, U.S. Pub. No. 2007/0293781 (Sims).
7. Claim 13 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Tupin, U.S. Pub. No. 2011/0060215 (Tupin).

Applicant, in view of at least the current further amendments to claim 1, traverses the grounds for each and every rejection for at least the reasons set forth herein below. Applicant addresses the specific rejections in the order they arise in the Office Action.
Applicant's Specific Responses to the Grounds for Rejection 1. Rejection of Claims 1-5 and 11 as anticipated by Mahajan

Applicant, in view of the current further clarifying amendments to each independent claim, traverses the rejection of claims 1-5 and 11, as being anticipated by the teachings of Mahajan. A proper case of anticipation cannot be established with regard to any one of the currently pending claims since the teachings of the cited Mahajan reference do not describe each recited element of any currently pending independent claim. Notably, Mahajan does not describe Applicant's clarified first and second conductive electrodes that are positioned on the belt and operate in a functionally similar manner that facilitates using the two distinct signals obtained by the first and second nodes to provide a filtered output signal enabling electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm.
Moreover, a proper reason cannot be established for one skilled in the art to modify

Mahajan's teachings, in a way that would result in Applicant's claimed invention. Notably, none of the references cited in the Office action demonstrates any awareness of a particularized problem that would provide a reason to modify Mahajan in a way that resulted in Applicant's claimed invention.
a. Applicant's Claimed Invention
Applicant's claimed invention is directed to a wearable device including a particular

electrode arrangement that facilitates monitoring vital signs (i.e., carrying out electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm) of its wearer. In particular currently amended claim 1, provided in clean form below, recites:
A wearable device for monitoring one or more vital signs of a human
body, the wearable device comprising:
a carrier configured to fit, while in use, fully around the human body, at an
abdominal part thereof; and
an electrode arrangement comprising a plurality of conductive electrodes
including one or more first electrode and one or more second electrode, wherein the plurality of conductive electrodes are arranged on the carrier to be brought in
contact with a skin of the body in use, and wherein all electrodes of the plurality of conductive electrodes are configured for operating simultaneously to receive
electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling monitoring of a
membrane potential of one or more muscles in the body,
wherein the one or more first electrode is arranged on the carrier to be in
contact with a side part of a torso of the body near the thoracic diaphragm, the one
or more first electrode being configured to cooperatively receive a first electrical
signal indicative of a membrane potential of a thoracic diaphragm of the body and
for providing the first electrical signal as a measurement signal;
wherein each electrode of the one or more second electrode and the one or
more first electrode is arranged aligned on the belt, such that the one or more
second electrode is aligned with the one or more first electrode, the at least one
second electrode thereby being arranged for receiving a second electrical signal
indicative of one or more further electric physiologic signals from the body,
wherein the second electrical signal in particular is indicative of a
further membrane potential, and
wherein the one or more second electrode is arranged for providing the
second electrical signal separate from the first electrical signal, the second electrode thereby providing a filter signal, for enabling filtering of the first
electrical signal using the second electrical signal for enabling electromyography
of the thoracic diaphragm. (Emphasis added).

Thus, Applicant's claimed invention, as presented in further-clarified independent claim 1, recites first and second conductive electrodes that, while obtaining different signals, are nevertheless configured to operate substantially the same way by "operating simultaneously to receive electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling monitoring of a membrane potential of one or more muscles in the body." (Emphasis added). As a result, the signals provided by the first conductive electrode and the second conductive electrode are directly comparable to each other. As such, the first electrical signal obtained from the one or more first electrode can be directly and straightforwardly filtered by the second electrical signal from the one or more second conductive electrode. The resulting filtered signal is a very weak diaphragmatic signal that (as a result of the filtering provided by comparing the two signals) nevertheless is measurable.

Applicant's disclosed/claimed invention thus addresses an underlying problem of EMG signals of the diaphragm being very difficult to obtain because of the many sources of noise (heart, organs, other muscles, etc.) proximate the signal source. Moreover, the disclosed/claimed invention is based on an insight that the shape of the diaphragm can be used to the benefit of
improving measurability and accuracy of EMG measurements of diaphragmatic movement. See Applicant's FIGs. 2A, 2B and 2C; and corresponding written description at page 12, line 22 to page 13, line 12.

Importantly, contrary to Applicant's disclosed/claimed invention, Mahajan does not describe obtaining a diaphragmatic EMG signal. Thus, Mahajan does not anticipate Applicant's currently clarified claimed invention.
b. The cited reference does not anticipate Applicant's claimed invention
Applicant, in view of the current clarifying amendment to independent claim 1, traverses the rejection of independent claim 1 that recite substantially the same combination of elements.
Mahajan, upon which the current rejection of independent claim 1 solely relies,

describes a device that does not obtain a diaphragmatic EMG signal. Mahajan in paragraph [0070] refers to "diaphragmatic expansion sensors" that perform a "measurement of strain." Such strain measurements enable sensing diaphragmatic expansion by "measurement of changes in girth or displacement of the upper and lower abdomen." Mahajan, indeed, mentions EMG sensors. However Mahajan describes using the EMG sensors to measure organ function drive. See Mahajan, at paragraph [0074]. None of the paragraphs cited in the Office action [0063], [0070] and [0074] describes using the EMG sensors to provide a diaphragmatic EMG signal output measurement. For at least this reason, Mahajan does not anticipate Applicant's now- clarified claimed invention.

Applicant adds that claim 1 is now clarified and recites a combination of features that unequivocally describe Applicant's claimed invention as having first and second conductive electrodes that are of a same type/physical alignment such that both are configured for providing comparable membrane potential signals to facilitate providing the claimed diaphragmatic EMG signal output measurement.
Thus, for at least the above-provided reasons, Applicant's invention recited in claim 1 is not anticipated by the teachings of Mahajan.
c. The dependent claims are not rendered obvious by the cited reference's teaching
Claims 2-5 and 11 depend from independent claim 1, respectively, and incorporate each of the elements discussed herein above that are neither described nor suggested in Mahajan.
Applicant traverses the rejection of dependent claims 2-5 and 11 for at least the reasons discussed above with reference to claim 1.

Applicant reserves the right to provide additional reasons for distinguishing claims 2-5 and 11 from the teachings of the prior art in the event that any further Office action recites new grounds for rejecting claims 2-5 and 11, or any claim from which claims 2-5 and 11 depend.
